title: 1 Kings 7:13–22
context: The narrative returns to the LORD’s house. Solomon brings Hiram, a skilled bronze worker from Tyre, who should not be confused with Hiram king of Tyre (5:1). He casts two bronze pillars with ornamented capitals and sets them at the porch of the temple, naming the right pillar Jachin and the left Boaz (7:21). The text does not explain the names, and this page does not build an argument on them. Parallel accounts differ in some details, stated here without harmonization: 1 Kings 7:14 calls Hiram the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, while 2 Chronicles 2:13–14 calls him Huram-abi, the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan (“abi” means “his father”). 1 Kings 7:15 gives each pillar a height of eighteen cubits, as do 2 Kings 25:17 and Jeremiah 52:21, while 2 Chronicles 3:15 gives thirty-five cubits. 1 Kings 7:16 and Jeremiah 52:22 give each capital five cubits, while 2 Kings 25:17 gives three. 2 Chronicles 3:16 mentions one hundred pomegranates on chains, while 1 Kings 7:20 mentions two hundred around a capital and 7:42 four hundred for the two networks (as does 2 Chronicles 4:13). Both traditions read the unit as constructive description of skilled work offered for the LORD’s house.

verses.text: King Solomon sent and brought Hiram out of Tyre.
verses.arminianNotes: King Solomon sends for Hiram of Tyre. Arminian readers note that the work of the LORD’s house draws on a skilled worker from beyond Israel’s borders, through the friendly relations between Solomon and Tyre (5:1, 12). Human initiative and cooperation are real means by which the house is built.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence in bringing the right craftsman from Tyre at the right time, through the peace and treaty God had granted (5:12). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God accomplishes his purposes through ordinary human decisions, alliances, and skills, and that Gentile hands can serve his house.

verses.text: He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze; and he was filled with wisdom and understanding and skill to work all works in bronze. He came to King Solomon and performed all his work.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram, son of a widow of Naphtali and a Tyrian father, is “filled with wisdom and understanding and skill” for bronze work. Arminian readers see this as God-given ability that Hiram freely develops and applies. The language recalls Bezalel’s gifting for the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3), though 1 Kings does not mention the Spirit here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Hiram’s skill as God’s gift, as with Bezalel, whom God filled for the tabernacle work (Exodus 31:3). Common gifts of craft are distributed by God for the good of his people and for his worship. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that skill in the arts comes from God and that using it in his service is a fitting response.

verses.text: For he fashioned the two pillars of bronze, eighteen cubits high apiece; and a line of twelve cubits encircled either of them.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram fashions two bronze pillars, eighteen cubits high, with a circumference of twelve cubits. Arminian readers note the scale and craftsmanship and do not press the numbers for symbolism. The parallel at 2 Chronicles 3:15 gives a different height, which this page records in the context without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the dimensions as historical description and decline to build doctrine on them. They note that Scripture preserves such details as part of a real account of a real building. Shared ground: both traditions receive the verse as describing a monumental work of skill, and both acknowledge the parallel difference honestly.

verses.text: He made two capitals of molten bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: Two capitals of molten bronze, each five cubits high, crown the pillars. Arminian readers see the narrator inviting admiration for skilled human work offered to God. The repetition of “five cubits” for each capital stresses symmetry and completeness rather than any coded meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the capitals as part of the beauty of the LORD’s house. They note that the narrator dwells on the work because the house was to be glorious, worthy of the name of the LORD (5:5). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as description of ornamented craftsmanship, without allegory.

verses.text: There were nets of checker work and wreaths of chain work for the capitals which were on the top of the pillars: seven for the one capital, and seven for the other capital.
verses.arminianNotes: Nets of checker work and wreaths of chain work adorn the capitals, seven for each. Arminian readers see intricate decoration that took time, skill, and care. They read the number seven as a simple count in the description and do not build a theological argument on it, since the text gives no explanation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the nets and wreaths as decorative detail. Some interpreters have proposed symbolic meanings for the numbers, but the text itself does not supply them. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as craft description and affirm that beauty in worship spaces can honor God without needing hidden codes.

verses.text: So he made the pillars; and there were two rows of pomegranates around the one network, to cover the capitals that were on the top of the pillars; and he did so for the other capital.
verses.arminianNotes: Two rows of pomegranates surround the network on each capital. Arminian readers note that pomegranates also decorated the hem of the high priest’s robe in the tabernacle instructions, suggesting continuity of worship imagery, but they do not press the comparison beyond what the text says.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also notice the pomegranate motif and its place in Israel’s worship imagery, while resisting a fixed allegorical meaning. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing ornamentation that fits the beauty of the LORD’s house, and both are cautious about assigning meanings the narrator does not state.

verses.text: The capitals that were on the top of the pillars in the porch were of lily work, four cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: The capitals on the pillars in the porch are of lily work, four cubits. Arminian readers see further evidence of careful, beautiful design. The flower motif, which recurs on the sea’s brim (7:26), points to a consistent artistic vision across Hiram’s work, carried out with real skill and freedom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lily work as part of the beauty appropriate to the LORD’s house. They note that God, who adorns the created world, is honored when human craft reflects that beauty. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as description of decorative work and decline to allegorize the lily pattern.

verses.text: There were capitals above also on the two pillars, close by the belly which was beside the network. There were two hundred pomegranates in rows around the other capital.
verses.arminianNotes: The capitals have two hundred pomegranates in rows around each, close by the network. Arminian readers note the abundance of decoration and the narrator’s care in recording it. The numbers differ from 2 Chronicles 3:16, which the context records plainly, and they see no need to force agreement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the profusion of detail and treat the verse as straightforward description of the capitals. Shared ground: both traditions receive the description as part of the historical record of the temple’s construction, and both acknowledge the parallel difference without speculation.

verses.text: He set up the pillars at the porch of the temple. He set up the right pillar and called its name Jachin; and he set up the left pillar and called its name Boaz.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram sets up the pillars at the porch and names them Jachin and Boaz. Arminian readers note that the text gives no explanation of the names, and they are content to leave them unexplained rather than build on a guess. The pillars mark the entrance of the house where Israel would meet the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the narrator records the names without comment. Interpretations of their meaning vary, and the text does not settle them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as marking the threshold of the LORD’s house and decline to make the names the basis of a theological argument.

verses.text: On the tops of the pillars was lily work. So the work of the pillars was finished.
verses.arminianNotes: Lily work on the tops of the pillars completes them: “So the work of the pillars was finished.” Arminian readers note the satisfaction of a task carried through to the end by skilled, willing workers. Faithful completion of a task is itself a form of service to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the completion formula the narrator’s steady progression toward the finished house (7:51). God brings the work to completion through the means he provides. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a simple statement of completion and affirm that diligent work done for God’s house is good.
